title: the Lower Danube Rising
premise: In 1916, Silas Ravensworth drives for suffragist Edith Marlowe along the Lower Danube trade routes, secretly reading the letters he carries and keeping a private ledger of what people confess to paper. When a census taker's probing questions expose a hidden community of displaced families, Silas is conscripted by officials to help document them — and realizes the records will be falsified to erase them. He races to smuggle the true testimony to a foreign correspondent before the victors' historians seal the official version. In the end he saves the record but loses his position, finding instead a found family among the displaced who teach him that memory, carried together, weighs less than guilt.
about_author: Yara Winterbourne is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing letters never meant to be read. She writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Silas Ravensworth, driver and secret reader of letters, introduces his philosophy: measure life by what fits in a satchel. Delivering mail along the Danube for suffragist Edith Marlowe, he catalogs confessions in a hidden ledger. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: controlled detachment beginning to crack as one letter makes him weep behind the wheel.

chapters.title: The Census Taker's Question
chapters.summary: A census taker named Herr Vogel asks Silas about households on a route that officially holds no one. Silas lies badly; Vogel writes something down anyway. Edith warns him that paperwork is how empires swallow people. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: first dread — the ledger he keeps mirrors the ledgers kept on him.

chapters.title: The Village That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Silas discovers a settlement of displaced families living off the census rolls, sustained by letters he himself has delivered. Their matriarch, Ana, recognizes him as the reader of their words. POV: Silas, with Ana's recounted memories. Emotional beat: shame transmuting into belonging — he has been their lifeline without knowing it.

chapters.title: Orders
chapters.summary: Officials conscript Silas to assist the census verification, threatening Edith's standing if he refuses. He must walk door to door recording the very people he's been protecting. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: complicity — the price of survival is paid in someone else's name.

chapters.title: Ana's Testimony
chapters.summary: Ana offers her story formally, asking Silas to write it exactly, including the parts that indict him. Her daughter Mila teaches him that memory spoken aloud weighs nothing but cannot be confiscated. POV: Silas with embedded testimony. Emotional beat: the ledger becomes an act of witness rather than theft.

chapters.title: Vogel's Ledger
chapters.summary: Silas finds Vogel's master file: names struck through, villages marked 'uninhabited,' a template for erasure already stamped. Vogel, weary, hints he was once recorded out of existence himself. POV: Silas, then a rare Vogel passage. Emotional beat: horror at the machinery, and uneasy recognition of the man inside it.

chapters.title: The Correspondent
chapters.summary: Edith connects Silas to Ruth Kessler, a foreign correspondent who can publish the truth before official histories harden. But moving the testimony means moving people, and the roads are closing. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: hope sharpening into urgency — time is now a physical weight.

chapters.title: Everything We Could Not Carry
chapters.summary: The settlement is raided ahead of schedule. Silas burns his own safe passage papers to forge transit documents for Ana's family, staying behind to guard the testimony. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: sacrifice — he finally measures himself not by what he carries but by what he gives up.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Cornered at a river checkpoint, Silas reads the testimony aloud to the young clerk sent to stop him, making the clerk a witness who must choose. The clerk lets the packet pass. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: climax — truth as contagion, passed hand to hand faster than any empire can burn it.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Kessler publishes; the victors' version cracks at the seams though it costs Silas everything formal — job, papers, country. Reunited with Ana's family in a new town, he opens a fresh ledger and writes their names first. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: resolution — memory shared is survival, and found family is what remains when everything else is carried away.
